notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Romans 5, based on the pages I was able to read from the approved sites. I note where I was unable to reach certain traditions or perspectives due to search/fetch limits.

---

## Romans 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1

**Traditional Reading:** Paul transitions from doctrine to application. “Therefore, having been justified by faith” (Greek aorist passive participle) looks back on a completed, once-for-all legal declaration by God — the believer stands acquitted. The first benefit flowing from this is **“peace with God.”** This is objective, not subjective — it is not the “peace *of* God” (Phil. 4:7, an inner calm), but “peace *with* God” — the war between the sinner and God is over. David Guzik writes: “the battle between God and our self is finished — and He won, winning us.” This peace is **only** through our Lord Jesus Christ; He Himself *is* our peace (Eph. 2:14). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_5-1-2)

Spurgeon preached this as a matter of experience, not mere doctrine: the believer must “realize, feel, enjoy, and understand” this peace in the soul. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/romans-5.html)

**Textual Note:** There is a manuscript debate over “we have peace” (ἔχομεν) vs. “let us have peace” (ἔχωμεν). The Pulpit Commentary notes overwhelming manuscript support for the subjunctive “let us have,” but argues the indicative fits the descriptive (not hortatory) context better. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/5.htm)

---

### v. 2

**Traditional Reading:** The second benefit is **access** into a standing of grace. The Greek word προσᾶγωγή (*prosagōgē*) means “introduction” — like being ushered into the presence-chamber of a king. Leon Morris notes: “we do not come in our own strength, but need an ‘introducer’ — Christ.” This access is permanent (perfect tense), a lasting privilege. Adam Clarke: “We are not brought to God for the purpose of an interview, but to remain with him.” Grace is not just the entry-point but the continuing principle of the Christian life. The third benefit is rejoicing (literally “boasting”) in the **hope of the glory of God**. “Hope” in Paul carries no uncertainty; J.B. Phillips translates it “happy certainty.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_5-1-2)

---

### v. 3

**Traditional Reading:** Paul anticipates the objection that hope is only for the future. He insists we also “glory in tribulations.” The word for tribulations (θλῖψις) is strong — “real hardships,” not minor inconveniences (Morris). Suffering is not a sign of God’s displeasure; for the believer it becomes a classroom. Spurgeon: “A Christian man should be willing to be tried… Do you want to be carried to heaven on a feather bed?” Martin Luther noted that tribulation develops whatever virtues it finds: if one is carnal it makes him more carnal; if spiritual, more spiritual. The natural result of affliction is impatience and rebellion; only the Spirit-wrought heart produces perseverance. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_54-5)

---

### v. 4

**Traditional Reading:** This is the “golden chain” of Christian growth: **tribulation → perseverance → proven character → hope**. Perseverance (ὑποϝονή, *hupomonē*) means literally “to abide under” — bearing up under trials in a God-honoring way, not a “grin and bear it” stoicism but a supernatural work of the Holy Spirit (Ironside). “Proven character” (δοκιμή, *dokimē*) was used in secular Greek for metals tested by fire and found pure. When faith passes through the furnace and endures, the believer gains a sense of authenticity — proof that faith is real. John Calvin: perseverance is “not the natural effect of tribulation; for we see that a great portion of mankind are thereby instigated to murmur against God.” Only the Spirit produces this. John Piper explains that proven character strengthens hope because it overcomes the fear that one is a hypocrite: when faith survives testing, the believer gains assurance of being a genuine child of God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_54-5)

---

### v. 5

**Traditional Reading:** **Hope does not disappoint** (or “put to shame”). Why? Because **“the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit.”** This is not merely a logical inference from Christ’s death (though that is true); it is a Spirit-given inner experience. John Piper distinguishes: “God’s love poured into your heart is not the same as God’s love proven to your mind… It is something felt in the heart.” Yet it has factual, objective content rooted in the cross. Paul transitions here from faith (v.1-2) to hope (v.2, 4-5) to love (v.5) — the classic triad. Every believer has the Holy Spirit (Rom. 8:9), but not every believer walks in the fullness of the Spirit (Eph. 5:18). Spurgeon: “The love of God is like light to a blind eye until the Holy Ghost opens that eye.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_54-5; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/how-to-experience-the-outpouring-of-gods-love)

---

### v. 6

**Traditional Reading:** Paul now demonstrates *why* God’s love is such sure ground for hope. Christ died for us when we were **“still without strength”** (ἀσθενής, *asthenēs* — helpless, powerless, morally incapacitated). We could do nothing to save ourselves. He died **“at just the right time”** (κατὰ καιρόν) — God’s strategic moment in redemptive history, when the world was prepared spiritually, linguistically, politically, and geographically (Gal. 4:4). And He died **“for the ungodly”** — not for the deserving. Hodge: “The Scriptures represent God’s love to sinners as independent of the work of Christ, and as preceding it.” Christ’s death does not procure a reluctant Father’s love; it expresses it. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_56-11; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

---

### v. 7

**Traditional Reading:** Paul illustrates the rarity of sacrificial death. **“Scarcely for a righteous man will one die”** — a merely just, upright person rarely inspires such devotion. **“Though for a good man someone might possibly dare to die”** — the “good” man (ἀγαθός) goes beyond righteousness by being kind, benevolent, and warm-hearted. The point: even the highest human love barely stretches to die for the *best* of people. Christ died for the *worst*. Gill notes this contrast heightens the unparalleled nature of divine love. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/5.htm; https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_56-11)

---

### v. 8

**Traditional Reading:** The ultimate proof: **“God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”** The demonstration is not primarily *that* Jesus died, but *for whom* — for sinners, the ungodly, those in active rebellion. Spurgeon: “If Christ died for the ungodly, this fact leaves the ungodly no excuse if they do not come to him.” The cross is simultaneously the ultimate demonstration of God’s love and the ultimate demonstration of man’s hatred — yet the height of man’s hatred cannot defeat the height of God’s love. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

---

### v. 9

**Traditional Reading:** Paul now argues from the greater to the lesser (a fortiori): if God has already done the hard thing (**justified us by Christ’s blood**), He will certainly do the comparatively easier thing (**save us from wrath** through Him). John Trapp: “It is a greater work of God to bring men to grace, than, being in the state of grace, to bring them to glory; because sin is far more distant from grace than grace is from glory.” The “wrath” here is God’s righteous, eschatological wrath — the final judgment from which believers are delivered. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/much-more-shall-we-be-saved-by-his-life)

---

### v. 10

**Traditional Reading:** The a fortiori argument continues: **“If when we were enemies we were reconciled… through the death of His Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through His life!”** John Piper draws out that God the Father is the primary actor — we “were reconciled *to God* through the death of *His Son*.” The Father did not need persuading; He initiated. The logic: if He loved us enough to reconcile us when we were enemies, He will certainly complete our salvation now that we are friends. “Saved by His life” points to Christ’s ongoing resurrected life and intercession (cf. Heb. 7:25). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/much-more-shall-we-be-saved-by-his-life)

---

### v. 11

**Traditional Reading:** The climax of the first section: **“We also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation.”** Spurgeon preached this as “a high attainment in spiritual life” — not merely rejoicing in salvation (an early experience) or in tribulation (a riper fruit), but rejoicing *in God Himself*. This “touches the confines of heaven.” The word translated “reconciliation” (καταλλάγη) means an exchange — enmity replaced with peace. It is something “received,” not achieved. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/; https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/joy-in-a-reconciled-god)

---

### v. 12

**Traditional Reading:** Paul shifts to the basis of justification, contrasting two representative heads: Adam and Christ. **Sin entered the world through one man** (Adam, not Eve — 1 Tim. 2:14 notes Adam sinned with full knowledge). **Death through sin**, and death **passed to all men, because all sinned**. David Guzik: Adam and Eve were real, historical people — Paul treats Genesis 3 as fact, and “you can’t take away the truth of Genesis 3 without taking away principles that lay the foundation for our salvation.” The phrase “because all sinned” (ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον) has been interpreted variously: (a) all sinned *in Adam* (Augustine, Reformed federal headship); (b) all sinned individually, following Adam’s pattern. Guzik takes the federal headship view: all humanity was seminally present in Adam and shares in his guilt. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

---

### v. 13

**Traditional Reading:** Paul explains that **sin was in the world before the Law** (of Moses) was given. The period from Adam to Moses proves that sin and death reigned apart from the Mosaic Law. **“Sin is not taken into account when there is no law”** — meaning not that sin doesn’t exist, but that it is not formally imputed or charged in the same judicial manner as under a codified law. Yet death still reigned (v.14), proving that sin was real and counted against humanity even without the Mosaic Law. Gill: this demonstrates there was a law before Moses (the law written on the heart, or the command given to Adam), otherwise sin could not be reckoned. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/5.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

---

### v. 14

**Traditional Reading:** **Death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the way Adam transgressed** — meaning those (like infants) who did not personally violate a direct divine command as Adam did. This proves that Adam’s sin had corporate consequences for the whole race. Adam is a **“pattern”** (τύπος, *typos*) of the One to come — Christ. Both are federal heads whose single act determines the destiny of those they represent. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

---

### v. 15

**Traditional Reading:** **“But the gift is not like the trespass.”** Paul begins a series of contrasts showing that while Adam and Christ are parallel as representatives, Christ’s work far exceeds Adam’s. **“If the many died by the trespass of the one man, how much more did God’s grace and the gift… abound to the many!”** The “much more” (πολλῷ μᾶλλον) is a key phrase. Adam’s one act brought death to all connected to him; Christ’s gift brings life far more abundantly. Grace “super-abounds” beyond the damage of sin. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

---

### v. 16

**Traditional Reading:** Another contrast: **“The judgment followed one sin and brought condemnation”** — Adam’s single trespass was enough to condemn all. **“But the gift followed many trespasses and brought justification”** — Christ’s gift not only covers Adam’s one sin but the multitude of sins accumulated by humanity. Gill: “the righteousness of Christ is not only a justification of his seed from that one offence, but from all others.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/romans/5.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

---

### v. 17

**Traditional Reading:** **“If by the trespass of the one man, death reigned through that one man, how much more will those who receive an abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ!”** Believers do not merely escape death — they **reign in life**. This is a present reality, not only future. Note the emphasis on **“receiving”** — grace is received, not earned. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

---

### v. 18

**Traditional Reading:** Paul summarizes the parallel: **“Just as one trespass brought condemnation for all men, so also one act of righteousness brought justification and life for all men.”** The two “all men” groups must be interpreted in context. The first “all men” refers to all who are in Adam (every human being); the second “all men” refers to all who are in Christ (believers). This is not universalism — Paul is speaking of two corporate headships, and the scope of each “all” is defined by connection to the respective head. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

---

### v. 19

**Traditional Reading:** **“For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous.”** This verse clarifies the mechanism: **imputation**. Adam’s disobedience is credited (imputed) to those in him, making them sinners. Christ’s obedience (His whole life of obedience culminating in the cross) is credited to those in Him, making them righteous. This is the classic Protestant doctrine of imputed righteousness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

---

### v. 20

**Traditional Reading:** **“The Law came in so that the trespass would increase.”** This is a striking statement: the Law was given not to save but to make sin more evident and even to provoke its increase — “that the offense might abound” (KJV). The Law exposes and magnifies sin by providing a clear standard of God’s holiness. **“But where sin increased, grace increased all the more”** — the Greek verb ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν (*hypereperisseusen*) means grace “super-abounded.” Guzik: “We cannot out-sin the forgiveness of God, though we can reject it.” This verse is a cornerstone of the Lutheran law-gospel dialectic, though the specific Lutheran reading could not be fetched from LCMS or 1517.org due to search limits. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

---

### v. 21

**Traditional Reading:** The chapter concludes with the grand contrast: **“Just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”** Two empires: sin’s reign ends in death; grace’s reign brings eternal life. Grace does not merely cancel sin — it **reigns**. And it reigns “through righteousness” — the righteousness of Christ imputed to believers. The entire chapter moves from peace with God (v.1) to reigning in life through Christ (v.17) to grace reigning unto eternal life (v.21). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

---

## Denominational Distinctives (where found)

**Reformed / Federal Headship (vv. 12–19):** David Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic-Reformed leaning) and the sources cited through Precept Austin strongly present the federal headship / covenant theology reading: Adam represented all humanity; his sin is imputed to all his natural descendants. Christ represents all who believe; His righteousness is imputed to them. This is the classic Reformed understanding. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (v. 5):** David Guzik (Enduring Word) emphasises the experiential dimension of the Spirit’s work — the love of God “poured out in our hearts” is something every Christian should *experience*, not merely know doctrinally. He stresses being “constantly filled with the Holy Spirit” and “walking in the Spirit” as keys to this awareness. John Piper (Reformed Baptist) likewise distinguishes between knowing God’s love by argument and *feeling* it by the Spirit. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-5/; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/how-to-experience-the-outpouring-of-gods-love)

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** Spurgeon’s sermon on Romans 5:1 emphasises the *experiential* dimension: justification by faith must be “realized, felt, enjoyed, and understood in the soul.” He also stresses substitution — “Christ the Substitute for sinners: Christ standing for men, and bearing the thunderbolts of the divine opposition to all sin.” On v.8, Spurgeon emphasises that Christ died for those who are “wholly lost,” not “partly lost.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/romans-5.html)

- **Methodist/Wesleyan distinctives** (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com) — e.g., emphasis on the Spirit’s witness in v.5 and whether vv.12–19 support prevenient grace
